extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proof techniques / discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for constructing and recognizing proofs by (ordinary) mathematical induction, strong induction, and proof by smallest counterexample, including when to use each technique and common tricks/pitfalls. Covers applications to inequalities, divisibility, recursive sequences (Fibonacci), graphs (trees), and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction (basic outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a family of statements S1,S2,S3,... by showing (1) the basis step: S1 is true; and (2) the inductive step: for any integer k>1, prove Sk => S_{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a rigorous method (not the same as informal inductive reasoning) that proves statements for every natural number. Use the domino analogy: showing the first domino falls and each domino forces the next to fall implies all fall. In the inductive step, assume Sk and use it to deduce S_{k+1} by direct algebraic manipulation or logical argument (examples include sums of powers and factorial identities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse mathematical induction with inductive (empirical) reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical induction is a rigorous deductive method that yields absolute certainty; it is distinct from inductive (empirical) reasoning which infers likelihood from repeated observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize rigor: a correctly executed induction proof establishes truth for all relevant integers, unlike empirical pattern-spotting which suggests but does not prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction for statements with extra parameters (P(n,x) style)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving statements of the form 'for every n in N, P(n,x) holds for all x satisfying some condition' (e.g., Bernoulli's inequality (1+x)^n >= 1+nx for all x>-1), perform the basis and inductive steps while keeping the extra variable and its conditions explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the inductive step you must ensure operations preserve the conditions on the extra variable (e.g., when multiplying both sides of an inequality by (1+x), verify (1+x)>0 so the inequality direction is preserved). State 'for all x with x>-1' in both basis and inductive step and show the implication holds uniformly in x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality induction trick: adding unequal quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: When working with inequalities you may add different quantities to each side provided you add a larger quantity to the larger side (e.g., if x<y and a<b then x+a < y+b). Also, if x<y and b>0, then x < y+b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these facts to manipulate inequalities in inductive steps (example used to amplify a power inequality by multiplying by 2 and then adding 1 to the larger side). Remember to justify sign/positivity conditions before multiplying or adding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong induction (outline and when to use it)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong induction: prove S1 (or the first several statements), then assume S1,S2,...,Sk are all true and show this collection of truths implies S_{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strong induction when Sk alone does not neatly yield S_{k+1}, but some earlier Sm (m<k) together imply S_{k+1}. The outline: (1) prove the initial base case(s); (2) for arbitrary k>1 assume S1..Sk and deduce S_{k+1}. Domino analogy extends: if the falling of the first k dominoes always makes domino k+1 fall, then all dominoes fall. Examples: divisibility statements where factoring fails under ordinary induction and structural arguments on trees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong induction often requires multiple base cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When the inductive implication uses an Sm with m appreciably smaller than k (e.g., k-5), the basis step must check all initial statements up to that offset (e.g., S1..S6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify how far back in the sequence you need to rely on previous statements in the inductive argument; include all those initial cases in the base verification. Example: proving 12 | (n^5 - n) required checking the first six positive integers as base cases before applying a k-5 implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose structures and apply induction to components
rubrics_metrics.description: For combinatorial or structural theorems (e.g., trees with n vertices have n-1 edges), remove or isolate a part of the object to produce smaller subobjects, apply the inductive hypothesis to each component, and recombine results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly describe the decomposition (e.g., remove an edge yielding two smaller trees T1 and T2 with x and y vertices), apply the inductive statement to each smaller piece (they have fewer than k+1 vertices), then count or combine to obtain the statement for the original object. Justify that the components satisfy the hypotheses of the inductive hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proof by smallest counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove all Sn are true, check S1, assume for contradiction that some Sn is false, let k be the smallest integer for which Sk is false; then S_{k-1} is true and Sk false — use that collision to derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a hybrid of induction and contradiction that often leads directly to a contradiction. Steps: (1) verify base case(s); (2) assume not all true; (3) choose minimal counterexample k; (4) use S_{k-1} (or other smaller true statements) together with the falsity of Sk to reach a contradiction. Note: many authors do not announce this technique explicitly; learn to recognize the pattern in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: If ordinary inductive factoring fails, consider strong induction or smallest counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: When attempting the inductive step you may be unable to factor or extract a needed common factor (e.g., trying to factor (k+1)^5-(k+1) to pull out 12 fails under ordinary induction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this failure as a signal to try strong induction (use several previously established statements) or the smallest counterexample method. The textbook shows how strong induction solves divisibility obstacles by relating (k+1) to (k-5) and then assembling polynomial terms divisible by 12.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurrence relations explicitly in induction on sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving identities involving recursively defined sequences (e.g., Fibonacci numbers where F_n = F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}), the recurrence is the natural tool and should be invoked in the inductive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to substitute the recurrence to rewrite F_{k+2} as F_{k+1}+F_k (or analogous forms) and then apply the inductive hypothesis to simplify to the desired expression (e.g., proving Cassini-type identities or limits of ratios). Make the use of the recurrence explicit in the algebraic manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check domain and sign conditions before algebraic operations in inductive steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Before multiplying both sides of an inequality or performing operations that could reverse inequality direction, verify any required positivity or other domain conditions (e.g., verify 1+x>0 when multiplying Bernoulli's inequality by 1+x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the condition (such as x>-1) in both basis and inductive steps, and justify that the operation is valid for all x in the allowed domain. Failure to check these can invalidate the inductive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show explicit algebraic manipulation; do not omit necessary intermediate steps
rubrics_metrics.description: In inductive steps demonstrate the algebraic transformations that convert the assumed expression (Sk) into the required expression (S_{k+1}) — e.g., expand, group terms, factor, or add/subtract terms as shown in factorial-sum and Fibonacci examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write down substitutions coming from the inductive hypothesis and show each algebraic manipulation that leads to the target. This makes the logical flow clear and prevents subtle errors (for instance, in divisibility proofs where factoring must be shown explicitly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use earlier proven propositions or number-theoretic facts inside induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage previously proved results (e.g., gcd properties and Bézout's identity) within base cases or inductive arguments to deduce divisibility or primality consequences (example: using Proposition 7.1 to show if p divides a product and gcd(p,a)=1 then p divides the other factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an inductive argument invokes algebraic or arithmetical facts, cite and apply the appropriate proposition/theorem. This is particularly useful in proofs about primes, divisibility, and uniqueness of factorization (as in the proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine techniques to handle existence and uniqueness theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: For some theorems you may need to combine strong induction (for existence) with proof by smallest counterexample (for uniqueness), as in the proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the proof in two stages: use strong induction to establish existence (every n>1 has a prime factorization), then use minimal-counterexample reasoning to show uniqueness by assuming a smallest n with two different factorizations and deriving a contradiction via divisibility properties (e.g., a prime dividing a product divides one of the primes).
